lead: Below its cracking moment a reinforced beam behaves as one elastic material, and above it the concrete under the neutral axis cracks and drops out. Both states are analysed with a transformed section: the steel is replaced by an equivalent area of concrete, m times larger, where m = E<sub>s</sub>/E<sub>c</sub> is the modular ratio. The uncracked transformed section gives the cracking moment M<sub>cr</sub>; the cracked one gives the service stresses and the stiffness used for crack widths and deflections. Only a few syllabi list this as a separate topic, but every deflection and crack check rests on it.
prereq: You need the elastic properties of concrete and steel, and the serviceability checks that use these results.

sections.h3: Modular ratio and the uncracked section

blocks.text: Steel and concrete at the same level have the same strain, so the steel stress is m times the concrete stress there. With E<sub>s</sub> = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm² and the short-term modulus E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√f<sub>ck</sub> (IS 456 clause 6.2.3.1), M25 gives E<sub>c</sub> = 25 000 N/mm² and m = 8. For the working stress method and for service-load stresses IS 456 uses m = 280/(3σcbc) instead (10.98 for M25, 13.33 for M20), which allows for creep under sustained load.

Before cracking, the whole concrete section b × D acts, and the steel adds (m − 1)A<sub>st</sub>: m A<sub>st</sub> carries the steel's force, minus the A<sub>st</sub> of concrete the bars already displace. The neutral axis ȳ (from the top) and the second moment of area I follow by taking moments of areas:
ȳ = [b D²/2 + (m − 1) A<sub>st</sub> d] / [b D + (m − 1) A<sub>st</sub>]     I = b D³/12 + b D (ȳ − D/2)² + (m − 1) A<sub>st</sub> (d − ȳ)²
blocks.where: b, D and d in mm; A<sub>st</sub> in mm²; I in mm⁴.

blocks.text: The first flexural crack opens when the bottom fibre reaches the flexural tensile strength f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√f<sub>ck</sub> (IS 456 clause 6.2.2). With y<sub>t</sub> = D − ȳ the distance from the neutral axis to that fibre:
M<sub>cr</sub> = f<sub>cr</sub> I / y<sub>t</sub>     (IS 456 Annex C: M<sub>r</sub> = f<sub>cr</sub> I<sub>gr</sub> / y<sub>t</sub> with the gross section, ignoring the steel)
blocks.where: M<sub>cr</sub> in N·mm. The transformed I gives a value about 15 % higher; the code's gross-section value is the one used in the deflection formula below.

blocks.text: In a normally designed beam M<sub>cr</sub> is well below the service moment, so at service load the beam is cracked over most of its span. That is why service stresses come from the cracked section.

Above M<sub>cr</sub> the concrete below the neutral axis is ignored and the steel becomes m A<sub>st</sub>. Moments of area about the cracked neutral axis, depth x, give a quadratic; then the cracked second moment I<sub>cr</sub> and the stresses follow:
b x²/2 = m A<sub>st</sub> (d − x)     I<sub>cr</sub> = b x³/3 + m A<sub>st</sub> (d − x)²     f<sub>c</sub> = M x/I<sub>cr</sub>     f<sub>s</sub> = m M (d − x)/I<sub>cr</sub>
blocks.where: f<sub>c</sub> is the concrete stress at the top fibre and f<sub>s</sub> the steel stress, both in N/mm², under the service moment M in N·mm. The lever arm is z = d − x/3.

blocks.text: The real stiffness lies between I<sub>cr</sub> and I<sub>gr</sub>, because the concrete between cracks still carries some tension. IS 456 Annex C gives an effective moment of inertia for short-term deflection:
I<sub>eff</sub> = I<sub>cr</sub> / [1.2 − (M<sub>r</sub>/M)(z/d)(1 − x/d)(b<sub>w</sub>/b)],   I<sub>cr</sub> ≤ I<sub>eff</sub> ≤ I<sub>gr</sub>
blocks.where: M is the largest service moment; b<sub>w</sub>/b = 1 for a rectangle. The short-term deflection of a simply supported beam under a uniform load w is then 5wL⁴/(384 E<sub>c</sub> I<sub>eff</sub>).

examples.question: A beam has b = 300 mm, D = 500 mm, d = 450 mm and A<sub>st</sub> = 1200 mm², in M25 concrete. Using E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√f<sub>ck</sub>, find m, the uncracked transformed section and the cracking moment, and compare it with the Annex C gross-section value.
steps: Annex C: M<sub>r</sub> = 3.5 × (300 × 500³/12)/250 = 3.5 × 3125 × 10⁶/250 = 43.75 kN·m. The steel raises the cracking moment by 15 %.
examples.answer: m = 8; ȳ = 260.6 mm, I = 3443 × 10⁶ mm⁴; M<sub>cr</sub> = 50.3 kN·m (gross section, as Annex C uses: 43.75 kN·m).

examples.question: The same beam spans 6 m, simply supported, and carries a service moment of 60 kN·m. With m = 8, find the cracked neutral axis, the concrete and steel stresses, I<sub>eff</sub> and the short-term midspan deflection.
steps: 60 kN·m > M<sub>r</sub> = 43.75 kN·m, so the beam is cracked.
Service load w = 8M/L² = 8 × 60/6² = 13.33 kN/m = 13.33 N/mm. Deflection = 5 × 13.33 × 6000⁴/(384 × 25 000 × 1594 × 10⁶) = 5.6 mm (with I<sub>gr</sub> it would be 2.9 mm, with I<sub>cr</sub> 7.5 mm).
examples.answer: x = 140.7 mm, f<sub>c</sub> = 7.05 N/mm², f<sub>s</sub> = 124.0 N/mm², I<sub>eff</sub> = 1594 × 10⁶ mm⁴; short-term deflection 5.6 mm, well inside 6000/250 = 24 mm before creep and shrinkage are added.

traps: Using m A<sub>st</sub> in the uncracked section. The bars displace concrete, so the added area is (m − 1)A<sub>st</sub>; m A<sub>st</sub> is right only in the cracked section, where the concrete around the bars is ignored.

Using I<sub>cr</sub> to compute M<sub>cr</sub>. M<sub>cr</sub> belongs to the uncracked section; with I<sub>cr</sub> = 1197 × 10⁶ mm⁴ the example would give a meaningless 'M<sub>cr</sub>' below 20 kN·m.
Taking y<sub>t</sub> = D/2 for the transformed section. The steel moves the axis down to 260.6 mm, so y<sub>t</sub> = 239.4 mm, not 250 mm.
Comparing M<sub>cr</sub> with the factored moment M<sub>u</sub>. M<sub>cr</sub> is a service-load quantity; compare it with the service moment.

Mixing the two modular ratios: E<sub>s</sub>/E<sub>c</sub> (8 for M25) for short-term elastic behaviour, 280/(3σcbc) (10.98 for M25) for the working stress method and service stresses. State which one you use.

quiz.q: Define the modular ratio and give the IS 456 working stress value for M20.
quiz.a: m = E<sub>s</sub>/E<sub>c</sub>, the ratio of the elastic moduli of steel and concrete. For working stress design m = 280/(3σcbc) = 280/(3 × 7) = 13.33 for M20.

quiz.q: Write the IS 456 flexural tensile strength of concrete.
Why is the tension steel transformed as (m − 1)A<sub>st</sub> before cracking but m A<sub>st</sub> after?
quiz.a: Before cracking the gross concrete area b × D already includes the space the bars fill, so only the extra (m − 1)A<sub>st</sub> is added. After cracking the tension concrete is ignored altogether, so the steel counts in full as m A<sub>st</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is a normally designed beam cracked at service load?
quiz.a: Its service moment is around M<sub>u</sub>/1.5, while M<sub>cr</sub> is set by the small tensile strength of concrete. In the worked example M<sub>r</sub> = 43.75 kN·m against a service moment of 60 kN·m.

quiz.q: For f<sub>ck</sub> = 30 N/mm², find E<sub>c</sub> and m (short-term).
A 230 × 450 mm beam (d = 402 mm) has 3 bars of 20 mm and m = 10.98. Find the cracked neutral axis depth.
Why does I<sub>eff</sub> in the second example come out nearer I<sub>cr</sub> than I<sub>gr</sub>?
quiz.a: The service moment (60 kN·m) is well above the cracking moment (43.75 kN·m), so most of the beam is cracked and tension stiffening adds only a little: I<sub>eff</sub> = 1594 × 10⁶ against I<sub>cr</sub> = 1197 × 10⁶ and I<sub>gr</sub> = 3125 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

quiz.q: If f<sub>ck</sub> rises from 25 to 30 N/mm² in the first example, what happens to M<sub>cr</sub>?
quiz.a: f<sub>cr</sub> rises from 3.5 to 3.83 N/mm² (√30 × 0.7), and m falls to 7.30, which moves ȳ slightly up. The f<sub>cr</sub> increase dominates, so M<sub>cr</sub> rises by about 9 %.

beyond: Not for the exam. Prestressed concrete is designed so that the section stays uncracked at service load, and then the uncracked transformed section of this chapter is the working tool. For long-term behaviour designers use an age-adjusted modular ratio, E<sub>s</sub>/[E<sub>c</sub>/(1 + χφ)], with the creep coefficient φ. Search for age-adjusted effective modulus and tension stiffening.
